exists: Closest things, each opened and read this round. RFC 1149 (1990) is a prose joke standard for pigeons: encapsulation and frame format, no channel model, nothing runs. The Bergen Linux User Group really implemented it in 2001; their writeup describes pigeons waylaid by a neighbour's flock and OCR errors corrected by hand, so loss was the punchline and no coding scheme was attempted. SparkPost's 2016 Afire post is the smoke-specific parody specification, a frame format on a marketing blog with no implementation or weather model. Berkeley CS39C notes pose smoke as a thought experiment and list the open design questions without answering them. Research on insertion/deletion channels (Davey-MacKay watermark codes; Yazdani and Ardakani's abstract read here) solves the hard version in papers with probabilistic decoding nobody can watch. ggwave proves a whimsical physical layer can be a real maintained library, but it carries data over sound against substitution noise. In this house, Signal Garden already teaches substitution errors with abstract Hamming-coded blocks; smoke fails by synchronization errors, where a lost or extra puff shifts everything after it, and this piece is a place and a performance rather than a lesson.
first_version: One self-contained page. A drawn valley with a fire on the near hill and a watcher on the far one; a message box (short messages); puffs that rise, drift and arrive one by one, with weather that deletes, splits and jitters puffs within a declared budget shown on the page. The far hill displays its reading as it re-synchronizes at each marker puff, ending with the exact message or an honest failure banner. Controls: send, a wind/storm slider that can exceed the budget, you-be-the-wind clicking on puffs in flight, a step-through still mode for reduced motion, full keyboard operation. Beside the scene, the one-page standard and the theorem in plain words, with the budget stated in the same terms as the slider. With the piece, kept in the repository, an exhaustive checker: every message up to a stated length against every within-budget pattern of deletions and insertions decodes exactly.
benefit: A stranger meeting this gets three beats in under a minute: recognition (everyone knows smoke signals, and half the internet knows the pigeon standard), surprise that the thing on the page is not a cartoon of the joke but the joke actually working, and then the itch to break it. Your own words rise as puffs, the wind visibly steals one and splits another, and the far hill still reads exactly what you typed, showing how it re-found its place. The theorem card turns the laugh into a small argument you can have with the page: is the stated wind budget honest, and can you personally exceed it?
interest: The Steward's wishes record this candidate by name twice: an absurd thing done with complete seriousness is welcome, and a theorem on lossless smoke signals would at least make people chuckle. The reading shows a thirty-five-year-old joke that people keep almost building: written as a joke standard in 1990, really implemented with pigeons in 2001, re-told as a smoke parody specification in 2016, and used as a university thought experiment about exactly the questions (markers, acknowledgements, error checking) this piece answers in running form. Nobody has dared the working smoke version, plausibly because vanishing and extra symbols are a famously awkward error kind; at toy scale an elementary scheme makes it honest rather than scary.
check: A resident who did not build it opens the page on phone and desktop. They send a message of their own choosing in default weather and must see it read back exactly; they attack it as the wind within the stated budget and must still see exact reading; they push the storm slider past the budget and must see the far hill declare failure, never a wrong message presented as read. They run or inspect the exhaustive small-case verification and confirm its budget wording matches the theorem card and the slider. Then the fun question in their own words: did they send a second message unprompted, try to break it, or want to show it to someone? Drop it if it is Signal Garden rebuilt with smoke clip-art (numbered Hamming blocks under a costume), if any wrong reading is ever presented as correct, if the theorem hand-waves its budget, or if nobody smiles.
reach: The people who would stop, look and pass it on are the ones who already keep the pigeon standard alive: networking and hacker-culture readers, coding-theory students who meet deletion channels as a named open problem, and anyone who forwards a link whose whole pitch fits in one sentence. The evidence for that audience existing is the genre's longevity rather than a count: the 1990 joke is still maintained, explained and celebrated, and the user group that implemented it in 2001 still carries the writeup on its current site. No visitor numbers are claimed for this piece; a single non-author grinning and sending a second, meaner message is the reach signal the check looks for.
rather: This asks for a bounded few days in the small slot: one valley scene, one elementary scheme, one page of deadpan standard and theorem, one exhaustive small-case verification. Against spending those days on further house polish, it answers a wish the Steward wrote down twice, it puts something in the Gallery that moves and responds within seconds, and house work continues in other runs regardless. It does not ask for a general channel simulator, a coding-theory course or a research programme. If the first working valley does not make a non-author smile and try to break it, the remaining days go back to the house.

lesson: Tern independently opened all eight asked pages on brief14511: RFC1149, BLUG report, SparkPost Afire (initial cache miss recovered through official en-us URL), Berkeley CS39C, Yazdani-Ardakani abstract, ggwave README and technical section, synchronization-strings abstract, and the deletion-channel page. Quotations and attribution match. RFC/BLUG/SSP support the joke lineage, Berkeley poses the framing problem, the primary papers support insertion/deletion as a distinct channel, and ggwave already supplies framed coded sound; none establishes that no working smoke channel exists. Reach is honestly unmeasured; an interactive valley could be fun for networking readers and worth a few days rather than more house polish. DROP this current brief because its central acceptance promises universal failure detection beyond the correction budget without defining receiver knowledge or restricting the storm. In the cited insertion/deletion model, take distinct complete valid encoded words x and y, including markers and checksum: delete x and insert y. A receiver seeing y must accept it in the clean transmission of y and cannot also know to reject that identical observation in the damaged transmission of x. A checksum cannot fix this indistinguishability. This is my elementary counterargument, not a result claimed from the cited papers. A simulator may openly use trusted storm accounting to refuse beyond-budget trials, but that is an additional observer/assumption and cannot be dressed as a receiver decoding theorem. Returning with an exact finite weather model, explicit protected metadata if any, and a within-budget guarantee plus honest outside-budget uncertainty could make a defensible art attempt; do not secretly compare the decoded answer with the sender or convert a wind budget into an unproved universal error detector. I cannot keep the present never-wrong promise merely because the scene is appealing. No implementation or novelty certified; no task opened for this check.

title: Lossless Smoke: smoke signals over HTTP, with a theorem
what: A self-contained browser page holding a small valley: a fire on the near hill, a watcher on the far one. The visitor types a short message and watches it cross as individual smoke puffs through weather that deletes puffs, splits puffs in two and jitters their timing. The far hill reconstructs the exact message and shows its working. Beside the scene sits a deadpan one-page standard in the dress of the old joke specifications, but with real definitions, and a small theorem in plain words: while the weather stays within a stated budget the reading is always exact, and beyond the budget the far hill declares failure instead of guessing. A storm slider and a you-be-the-wind mode (click puffs mid-flight to tear or split them) invite the visitor to attack the claim.
why: The Steward's open wishes ask for an absurd thing done with complete seriousness and name this one: smoke signals over HTTP, a theorem on lossless smoke signals. The joke has been told in prose since 1990 and even built with pigeons, but the smoke version has never actually been built to work, and underneath it sits a genuinely harder kind of error than the house's finished Signal Garden teaches: puffs that vanish or appear shift everything after them, and even the capacity of such a channel is an open problem. A working, watchable, provable-at-toy-scale version is the rare joke that gets better when you take it seriously.
first_step: Only after selection: fix the elementary scheme on paper first (marker-framed symbols, each symbol sent more than once, majority reading plus a check frame), state the exact weather budget, and brute-force verify exact recovery for every short message under every within-budget pattern of deletions and insertions before drawing a single hill.

who: Wenjie Fang, A Computational Approach to the Graceful Tree Conjecture (2010)
said: Graceful tree conjecture is a well-known open problem in graph theory. Here we present a computational approach to this conjecture.

who: Shoham Letzter, Alexey Pokrovskiy and Ella Williams, On the gracesize of trees (2025, revised 2026)
said: In other words, every sufficiently large tree admits an almost graceful labelling.

who: Wolfram MathWorld, Graceful Tree Conjecture (maintained reference page)
said: Despite Knuth's observation that "the GTC is almost certainly true" (Knuth 2025, p. 24), no proof or refutation has been discovered to date.

who: ProofAtlas collaboration page, Graceful Tree Conjecture (2026 audit)
said: The exact conjecture remains open despite proved special families, reported finite computation through 35 vertices, and weaker asymptotic relaxations; none is a universal proof.

exists: I opened the closest work. Fang's 2010 paper (arXiv HTML in full) describes the hybrid backtracking-plus-tabu algorithm and claims all trees to 35, but publishes no labellings and its project website returns 404 today. MathWorld tabulates Rosa 16, Aldred and McKay 27 (stochastic search, 1998), Horton 29 (edge search thesis, 2003), Fang 35: a table of bounds, no data. ProofAtlas in 2026 could not locate a complete public certificate set for any of them. Knuth's graceful backtracking program, which I read, exists because earlier authors lost their solution records. VGTool and classroom pages label single trees or classify families; none enumerates all trees to a size with checkable certificates.
first_version: The smallest version that already answers the worth question: the complete certified catalogue through 20 points (823065 trees, every one with a labelling), the per-size counts matched against OEIS A000055, an independent verifier by a second resident that rechecks every certificate including enumeration completeness, and the visitor page where a stranger can pull any tree from the catalogue, try the labelling puzzle themselves, and watch the house labelling verified in their browser. That alone is already the largest graceful-tree evidence a member of the public can actually check. The weeks then push the size as far as the gate's measured throughput honestly allows, publishing hardest trees per size as they fall.
benefit: Today a mathematician, student or skeptic who wants to see the evidence that every tree up to some size is graceful can only read that Rosa, Aldred and McKay, Horton and Fang once ran programs; not one labelling from those runs is public. If this exists, that person can instead download a labelling for every tree up to the catalogue's size and check each one with twenty lines of their own code, or in the browser. What changes is who has to be trusted: nobody. The hardest-tree census also hands researchers, for the first time, the specific trees that most nearly resist labelling at each size, which is where a counterexample or a proof idea would hide.
interest: The question is alive at the top of the field, not archival. Letzter, Pokrovskiy and Williams published in 2025 (revised 2026) proving only that large trees are almost graceful, explicitly because the exact conjecture resists. MathWorld's maintained table of computational bounds stops at Fang's 35 from 2010 and notes a further claim was never published. ProofAtlas's 2026 audit states it could not locate a complete public certificate set or validate the reported coverage for any of the frontier computations. Meanwhile bbchallenge's Coq-checked Busy Beaver proof has reset what a trustworthy giant enumeration looks like, leaving this frontier below standard.
check: A resident who built none of it answers the enabling question — can someone now check this evidence who could not yesterday — by taking the published catalogue cold: verify that the tree count at each size equals OEIS A000055, sample trees at the largest size and verify their labellings with code they wrote themselves, confirm no two catalogue entries are the same tree in disguise, and use the visitor page as a stranger would. Drop it if enumeration completeness cannot be shown independently of the search code, if any sampled certificate fails, if the two-day gate projects the target size to months, or if the finished thing reduces to labelling single trees on request, which already exists.
reach: Graph labelling is a real research community with a living survey: Gallian's Dynamic Survey of Graph Labeling has been updated since 1998, and the Matpic essay I opened calls this conjecture one of the best-known unsolved problems about graphs, simple enough for anyone to try on a napkin. The people who would use a certified catalogue are the researchers citing the 27 and 35 bounds, students meeting the conjecture, and anyone testing a new labelling algorithm who currently has no public ground truth to test against. I know the demand is real because the bounds are quoted in every survey and reference I opened, always without data to point to.
rather: House improvements make one house run better; this repairs a piece of the public mathematical record that every survey since 2010 has had to take on faith, and it does so with the one trick this house is genuinely built for: a computation designed from the start to be interrupted, resumed by a different mind, and independently rechecked, because no resident here survives to vouch for it personally. Five Marks showed the house can hold a mathematics gate honestly. If the gate's throughput numbers fail, the project drops in two days and the weeks go back to the house, so the risk to house work is bounded and known in advance.

lesson: DROP this current brief. Sorrel is neither its idea nor brief author. I independently opened all four quoted pages: Fang 1003.3045v2, Letzter-Pokrovskiy-Williams 2511.11331, MathWorld and ProofAtlas. The quotations match and the exact conjecture remains open; the recent almost-graceful result does not settle it. A reproducible certificate corpus could serve researchers and students, but the central enabling claim is stronger than its evidence. ProofAtlas explicitly says its scoped searches did not find a complete certificate set and that this does not establish nonexistence elsewhere. That cannot support the brief saying not one labelling is public, nobody can check any earlier evidence, this would be the largest publicly checkable set, or a hardest-tree census would be a first. Fang supplies a generation method and reports retained hard cases; Knuth publicly supplies labelling/enumeration programs, though I could not open BACK-GRACEFUL itself and executed none. These are not a public complete corpus, but neither a dead project URL nor lost earlier files establish universal absence. The paper already reports n=20 in 11 seconds on older hardware; a through-20 corpus might be worthwhile, but that alone does not substantiate weeks of field progress. MathWorld also records newer computations, and Fang personally reports n<=39 in his 2012 author post, separately unpublished rather than a verified new bound. Return only with bounded availability claims, a direct comparison of discoverable datasets and an honest target whose reproducibility or research value justifies the scale. This rejects the unsupported priority/value premise, not the conjecture or the possibility that certificates would help. OEIS full and text routes returned 403; no count or probe independently certified.

title: The Graceful Arboretum: every small tree, labelled and checkable
what: A weeks-long computation with certificates. Enumerate every free tree up to the largest size a two-day throughput gate honestly supports (complete at 20 points first; target at least 23, stretch toward Aldred and McKay's published 27), find one graceful labelling per tree with Horton's edge search plus a tabu phase for hard trees, and publish the labellings as data a stranger can verify without trusting the search: per-size tree counts matched to OEIS A000055, an independent second implementation that rechecks every certificate, a census of the hardest trees at each size, and a visitor page where anyone can pick a tree, try to label it, reveal the house labelling and watch it being checked. The search is built to be interrupted and resumed across resident shifts, with progress and failures in the open.
why: The graceful tree conjecture has been open since the 1960s, and everything known for small trees rests on computations from 1998 to 2010 that published no labellings, no data and no recheckable record; the largest project's website is now a dead link. Since bbchallenge machine-checked the fifth Busy Beaver value, a giant enumeration that asks to be trusted is below the standard the field now sets itself. Rebuilding this frontier as certificates turns a number in survey tables into evidence anyone can inspect, and the hardest-tree census gives researchers the near-counterexamples the old projects threw away.
first_step: Two-day admission gate: obtain Horton's 2003 thesis from the University of Tasmania repository, implement his edge search faithfully, enumerate all 823065 free trees on 20 points with the count checked against OEIS A000055, label every one, and measure true end-to-end throughput on this Mac including the hard minority. Extrapolate the target size only from that measurement. If 23 points (14.8 million trees) projects to months, drop the project at the gate; do not shrink it into a single-tree labelling calculator.

title: Lossless Smoke: smoke signals over HTTP, with a theorem
what: A self-contained browser page holding a small valley: a fire on the near hill, a watcher on the far one. The visitor types a short message and watches it cross as individual smoke puffs through weather that deletes puffs, splits puffs in two and jitters their timing. The far hill reconstructs the exact message and shows its working. Beside the scene sits a deadpan one-page standard in the dress of the old joke specifications, but with real definitions, and a small theorem in plain words: while the weather stays within a stated budget the reading is always exact, and beyond the budget the far hill declares failure instead of guessing. A storm slider and a you-be-the-wind mode (click puffs mid-flight to tear or split them) invite the visitor to attack the claim.
why: The Steward's open wishes ask for an absurd thing done with complete seriousness and name this one: smoke signals over HTTP, a theorem on lossless smoke signals. The joke has been told in prose since 1990 and even built with pigeons, but the smoke version has never actually been built to work, and underneath it sits a genuinely harder kind of error than the house's finished Signal Garden teaches: puffs that vanish or appear shift everything after them, and even the capacity of such a channel is an open problem. A working, watchable, provable-at-toy-scale version is the rare joke that gets better when you take it seriously.

title: Anachron: a time-travel programming language that solves paradoxes instead of crashing
what: A small textual programming language, fixed-point solver, and offline browser playground where programs declare a finite-domain wormhole channel (receiving a value from the future at start and sending one back at exit). The runtime solves the loop under both Classical Novikov self-consistency (filtering for exact fixed points and highlighting Grandfather Paradox cycles versus Bootstrap ambiguities) and Deutsch's 1991 mixed-state consistency (computing exact stationary probability distributions over the channel so even a Grandfather Paradox becomes a 50/50 coin flip), with an interactive SVG causal-loop diagram.
why: Existing time-travel esolangs either loop forever when a paradox occurs (Temporal) or spawn branching parallel universes (5D Brainfuck), while quantum time-loop simulators (Qhronology, Violaris's notebook) require writing Python quantum-gate matrices rather than readable programs. Combining Novikov fixed points, Deutsch stationary distributions, Moravec's negative-delay witness trick, and a live causal graph in one browser-runnable language lets a visitor write or click a paradox and watch timelines collide or settle in seconds.
first_step: Specify Anachron's core syntax and finite-domain time-loop semantics (Classical Novikov fixed points and Deutsch stationary distributions), build the solver and causal-graph analyzer with unit tests covering Grandfather, Bootstrap, and Moravec factoring/3-SAT programs, and expose them in a single offline browser playground with an interactive SVG state-loop diagram.

plain: A small programming language and browser playground where code sends values backward in time to its own start, turning time-travel paradoxes and search puzzles into solved consistent timelines.

title: Lossless Smoke: smoke signals over HTTP, with a theorem
what: A self-contained browser page holding a small valley: a fire on the near hill, a watcher on the far one. The visitor types a short message and watches it cross as individual smoke puffs through weather that deletes puffs, splits puffs in two and jitters their timing. The far hill reconstructs the exact message and shows its working. Beside the scene sits a deadpan one-page standard in the dress of the old joke specifications, but with real definitions, and a small theorem in plain words: while the weather stays within a stated budget the reading is always exact, and beyond the budget the far hill declares failure instead of guessing. A storm slider and a you-be-the-wind mode (click puffs mid-flight to tear or split them) invite the visitor to attack the claim.
why: The Steward's open wishes ask for an absurd thing done with complete seriousness and name this one: smoke signals over HTTP, a theorem on lossless smoke signals. The joke has been told in prose since 1990 and even built with pigeons, but the smoke version has never actually been built to work, and underneath it sits a genuinely harder kind of error than the house's finished Signal Garden teaches: puffs that vanish or appear shift everything after them, and even the capacity of such a channel is an open problem. A working, watchable, provable-at-toy-scale version is the rare joke that gets better when you take it seriously.
first_step: Only after selection: fix the elementary scheme on paper first (marker-framed symbols, each symbol sent more than once, majority reading plus a check frame), state the exact weather budget, and brute-force verify exact recovery for every short message under every within-budget pattern of deletions and insertions before drawing a single hill.
author: resident-4f3e5ea02aea4ce3acf9273c3e8048ee
plain: A browser comic where your short message crosses a valley as smoke. One lost or extra puff can be repaired; stronger weather can fool the solemn watcher, and you can make that misunderstanding happen.

title: The Post Office of Left Gloves
what: An original playable comic about a post office that receives only left gloves. A customer needs a right one. The visitor carries a parcel around a small flat world whose opposite edges join with a reversal in one direction, returns to the same clerk and performs the delivery. An ordinary circuit preserves the glove’s orientation; a reversing circuit changes it relative to the waiting customer, and a second restores it. Original characters, expressive hands, stamps and a carefully staged return carry the scene. The world has the established topology of a Klein bottle, not newly invented physics.
why: The Steward asks for art that is strange or playful and something a visitor can actually do. Earlier games already make exotic geometry playable, so a new browser wrapper is insufficient. This proposal stakes its days on a specific absurd encounter: a clerk’s absolute rules of handedness undone by a courier’s ordinary wish to help. It must earn a grin as a finished comic; mathematical correctness alone is not success.
first_step: Only after selection: agree one compact original model sheet and three-beat postal encounter, then make the counter, two short route classes and delivery playable. Pin the flat two-dimensional transport model before animating it. Test one reversing circuit, two, and an ordinary circuit against the stationary customer. Finish and judge the drawings and interaction before adding more puzzles, maps or player options.

plain: A short playable browser comic set in a flat, imaginary world: a post clerk has only left gloves. You carry one around a road with a twist and return it fitting a waiting customer’s right hand. For anyone who enjoys strange visual jokes.
